name: Treaty with the Chippewa, Red Lake and Pembina Bands, 1863 (Treaty of Old Crossing)
nations: Pembina Band of Ojibwe (today within the Turtle Mountain, White Earth and Little Shell communities)
promises: Article 3: $20,000 a year for twenty years, paid per capita after an enrollment, with up to $5,000 a year that the President could direct to agriculture, education and goods.
Article 4: no punishment for past offences, and a fund to settle traders' depredation claims, with any balance added to the bands' annuities.
Article 5: up to $150 a year to each chief out of the annuities, $500 to each chief at the first payment to build a house, and $5,000 for a road from Leech Lake to Red Lake.
Article 8: a 160-acre homestead within the ceded area for each qualifying adult mixed-blood relative.

breaches.what: In fixing the award, the Commission credited against the $3,369,726 value of the lands ceded in the Red River Valley and northwestern Minnesota the treaty-date value of what the United States paid, $512,518.43, and treated the consideration as unconscionable, as it had found in its 1958 valuation decision.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Red Lake, Pembina and White Earth Bands v. United States, Dockets 18-A, 113 and 191, 9 Ind. Cl. Comm. 457 (1961)

source.title: Red Lake, Pembina and White Earth Bands v. United States, Dockets 18-A, 113, 191, Opinion of the Commission, October 5, 1961
source.publisher: Oklahoma State University Library, Indian Claims Commission Decisions

compensation: The Commission's amended final award of April 24, 1964 gave $2,034,889.56 ($3,369,726 less $635,774.87 paid on the claim and $699,061.57 in gratuitous offsets): $1,797,761.74 to the Red Lake Band and $237,127.82 to the Pembina Band.
today: The Red Lake Nation holds the lands around Red Lake that it did not cede in 1863.

nationVoice.nation: Red Lake Nation (Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians)
nationVoice.summary: At the Nation's 2013 ceremony for the treaty's 150th anniversary, Chairman Floyd Jourdain said looking back at this part of the Nation's own history is a bitter pill to swallow but also a healing process; the Nation marks every October 2 as a holiday in its memory.

nationVoice.nation: Red Lake Nation (Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians)
nationVoice.summary: The Nation says the Red Lake Band successfully negotiated the Treaty of Old Crossing with the federal government, agreeing to cede lands in the Red River and Pembina areas, and that the United States later broke treaty promises in 1889.

openQuestions: The 1958 valuation opinion (6 Ind. Cl. Comm. 247, OSU pointers 268 and 200) that first held the consideration unconscionable and gives the acreage was not opened; the acreage ceded is left out until it is.
The 1863 treaty was amended by the Senate and supplemented by the treaty of April 12, 1864 (13 Stat. 689); the supplement's changes to the annuities were not compared.

The Red Lake Nation's own account of the treaty (redlakenation.org, Red Lake Nation News coverage of Old Crossing commemorations) was not opened. Turtle Mountain's later claims in Docket 113 (1970-1978) concern the Pembina share and are a lead.
The 'today' sentence is general and should be tied to a dated Red Lake source.

Audit 2026-11-08: the Article 5 promise corrected. The treaty gives each chief up to $150 a year from the annuities and $500 once to build a house; it has no "$500 a year for agriculture". The breach reworded so that the 1961 opinion is not presented as the first finding of unconscionability, which it attributes to the Commission's earlier decision.

plain.promised: $20,000 a year for twenty years, paid to each enrolled person, a road from Leech Lake to Red Lake, and a 160-acre homestead for each qualifying adult mixed-blood relative.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1961 that what the United States paid, $512,518.43 at its treaty-date value, was unconscionable for lands in the Red River Valley and northwestern Minnesota worth $3,369,726.
plain.today: The Commission's 1964 final award was $2,034,889.56: $1,797,761.74 to the Red Lake Band and $237,127.82 to the Pembina Band. Whether it was paid has not been traced. Red Lake holds the lands it did not cede.
